# C&I Loan Interest Rates: What Determines Your Price and How to Get a Better One


A bank quotes two businesses of the same size, in the same city, wildly different **C&I loan interest rates** for what looks like the same loan. The gap almost never comes down to luck. It comes down to a formula banks apply consistently, plus **C&I loan rate factors** specific to each borrower that shift where a business lands inside that formula. This guide covers current **commercial and industrial loan rates** , what sets them, and how to negotiate a better one.


For a broader look at how **C&I loans** work as a category, see our companion guide, Commercial & Industrial (C&I) Loans: What They Are & How They Work.


## How Banks Set C&I Loan Rates


Every **C&I loan rate** starts with the same two-part structure: a benchmark plus a spread. The benchmark is a published reference rate the bank does not control day to day; the spread is what the bank adds on top to price its own risk.


Most US banks still peg **C&I lending rates** to the **prime rate** , the base rate large banks charge their most creditworthy commercial customers, published daily by the Federal Reserve. Larger, more sophisticated **C&I loans** increasingly price off **SOFR** (the Secured Overnight Financing Rate), the benchmark that replaced LIBOR for floating-rate commercial lending. Either way, benchmark plus spread equals the rate a business actually pays.


A well-documented business with strong cash flow and solid collateral gets a tight spread, often just a point or two over the benchmark. A newer or thinly capitalized business pays a wider spread on the same benchmark, sometimes several points more.

## Current C&I Loan Rates: The Benchmark Data


The **Bank Prime Loan Rate** sat at 6.75% as of early September 2026, per the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, and remains the pricing floor most community and regional banks quote from for **current C&I loan rates** . It is the single most useful number for gauging **commercial and industrial loan rates** at a glance, since most banks price directly off it.


On the small-business side, the Kansas City Fed's Small Business Lending Survey for the first quarter of 2026 (the most recent release; no Q2 2026 edition has posted as of this writing) puts the median rate on new small-business term loans at urban banks between 6.7% fixed and 7.1% variable. Rural banks priced somewhat lower over the same period.


Lending standards have stayed loose. The Fed's Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey shows a net 0.0% of banks tightened standards on **C&I loans** to large and middle-market firms in the third quarter of 2026, a calmer environment than the tightening cycle of 2023 to 2024, and part of why spreads on well-qualified deals have held steady this year.


## What Moves Your C&I Loan Rate


The benchmark is the same for every borrower on a given day. The spread is not, and the main **C&I loan rate factors** below explain why it moves.


**Time in business.** Three to five years of clean financials underwrite with more confidence than eighteen months of history. Longer, cleaner history narrows the spread.


**Cash flow strength.** What matters is what is left after expenses and existing debt service, compared against the proposed payment. A comfortable cushion reads as lower risk, even at similar revenue.


**Collateral quality.** Real estate and equipment with a clear resale market secure the tightest pricing. Inventory and receivables still help, but they are harder to value and liquidate, so the discount is smaller.


**Loan type.** A revolving line of credit, a term loan, and a real estate-secured loan price differently, even at the same bank, for the same borrower. The next section covers why.


**Banking relationship.** A business that already keeps deposits and payroll at the lending bank often gets a better look than a new relationship walking in cold. This is one factor a borrower can build over time.


**Industry and concentration risk.** A bank already carrying several loans in one volatile sector, or seeing heavy tariff or supply chain exposure in a borrower's industry, prices that exposure into the spread no matter how clean the individual borrower looks on paper.


## Fixed vs Variable: Which Costs Less Over Time


Every **C&I loan rate** is either fixed for the life of the loan or variable, resetting periodically off the benchmark. Each fits a different kind of risk tolerance.


A fixed rate locks in payment certainty. It usually starts slightly higher than a comparable variable rate, since the bank gives up its ability to reprice if the benchmark rises. For a business that wants predictable payments over a multi-year term loan, that premium is often worth paying.


A variable rate starts lower and moves with the benchmark, so the payment can shrink in a falling-rate environment and grow in a rising one. It suits a shorter-term facility, or a[revolving line of credit](https://www.dripcapital.com/en-us/resources/blog/business-line-of-credit) a business expects to pay down quickly, more than a decade-long real estate loan.


## How to Get a Better C&I Loan Rate


A handful of concrete moves shift where a business lands inside the spread.


**Strengthen the financials before applying.** Clean, current statements and a clear explanation of[working capital](https://www.dripcapital.com/en-us/resources/finance-guides/working-capital) trends give a bank less reason to price in uncertainty.


**Offer more collateral.** Pledging additional equipment, receivables, or property can narrow the spread meaningfully on a term loan.


**Shop more than one bank.** Pricing on **C&I lending rates** varies more across banks than most borrowers expect. A second or third quote is often the fastest way to find a tighter spread.


**Consider a shorter term.** Shorter terms carry less rate risk for the bank, which can translate into better pricing on a fixed-rate structure.


**Build the banking relationship first.** Moving deposits and payroll to a lender ahead of a loan request often earns better treatment than approaching a bank cold.


None of this guarantees a specific outcome; every bank weighs these factors with its own formula. Strengthening any one of them still tends to help.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What Is a Good C&I Loan Rate?


A good rate depends on the benchmark at the time and the borrower's own risk profile, so there is no fixed number that applies across the board. As of September 2026, a well-qualified borrower typically lands within a point or two of the Bank Prime Loan Rate, currently 6.75%, while a newer or higher-risk borrower pays a wider spread on the same benchmark.


### Are C&I Loan Rates Fixed or Variable?


Both structures exist, and the choice usually depends on the loan type and the borrower's preference. Term loans and real estate loans often carry a fixed rate for payment certainty, while revolving lines of credit more commonly float against the prime rate or SOFR.


### Why Did My C&I Loan Rate Go Up?


A floating rate moves automatically whenever its underlying benchmark, prime or SOFR, resets, regardless of anything the borrower did. A rate can also rise at renewal if the bank reassesses the business's financials, collateral, or industry risk and finds any of the three has weakened since the last review.


### What Determines a C&I Loan Rate?


Every rate combines a benchmark, usually the prime rate or a SOFR-based index, with a spread the bank sets based on the borrower's risk: time in business, cash flow, collateral, loan type, and industry exposure all factor into that spread.


### Do C&I Loan Rates Vary by Loan Type?


Yes. Revolving lines of credit, term loans, and owner-occupied real estate loans typically price differently, even for the same borrower at the same bank, because each carries a different risk and repayment profile for the lender.
